a: the hand of the LORD was on him
p: The Hebrew speaks of Ezekiel in the third person; the Greek has 'on me'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and the hand of the LORD was on him there
readings.plain: the hand of the LORD was on him

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐγένετο ἐπ᾽ ἐμὲ χεὶρ Κυρίου
readings.en: and the hand of the LORD came on me
readings.plain: the hand of the LORD was on me

why: The sudden third person, in a chapter told in the first person, is the harder reading, and the Greek's 'me' would be the natural smoothing. The Plain follows the Hebrew; the note at 1:3 sets out why the voice may have changed.
b: The Greek here is Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete. No scroll preserves this verse among those read for this part.

a: like the sole of a calf's foot
t: A calf's foot or winged feet
p: The Greek has 'their feet were winged'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and the sole of their feet like the sole of a calf's foot
readings.plain: like the sole of a calf's foot

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete)
readings.en: and their feet were winged
readings.plain: and their feet were winged

why: The Hebrew has a clear sense and the picture of a hoof-like foot fits the ox face. The Greek may be paraphrasing, or reading the line in the light of the wings. The Plain follows the Hebrew.
b: No scroll preserves this verse among those read for this part (11QEzek has 1:8-10).

a: The living creatures ran out and ran back
t: A verse missing in the Greek
p: Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete, has no text for 1:14.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and the living creatures ran and returned, like the appearance of the flash
readings.plain: The living creatures ran out and ran back

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete)
readings.en: (the verse is not there)
readings.plain: (left out)

why: The Hebrew has the verse and it fits the movement of the creatures in 1:12-13. The Greek of Ezekiel is shorter than the Hebrew in many places, and a missing verse here may come from the Greek translator or from a shorter Hebrew text behind it; the Plain keeps the Hebrew.
b: Only Codex Vaticanus as printed by Swete was read for the Greek; other Greek manuscripts and the critical editions of Rahlfs and Ziegler were not checked for this verse.

a: Wherever the spirit was about to go
p: The Greek has 'where the cloud was' for 'where the spirit was to go'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QEzek-b (4Q74) preserves the end of the verse (the spirit of the living creature in the wheels)
readings.en: to where the spirit was to go there
readings.plain: Wherever the spirit was about to go

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete)
readings.orig: οὗ ἂν ἦν ἡ νεφέλη, ἐκεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ πορεύεσθαι
readings.en: where the cloud was, there the spirit was to go
readings.plain: Where the cloud was, the spirit was to go.

why: The Hebrew repeats 'the spirit' as the verse's own key word, and the Greek 'cloud' may be a mistake in copying or translating, or a picture drawn from 1:4. The Plain follows the Hebrew.
b: The scroll has only the last words of the verse. In the same verse the Greek reads 'a spirit of life' for 'the spirit of the living creature', which is in line with its smoothing of the singular.

a: was the likeness of a dome
p: One Qumran copy reads 'their likeness' above the creature's head.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); the Greek has 'a likeness'
readings.en: and a likeness over the heads of the living creature, a dome
readings.plain: was the likeness of a dome

readings.w: 4QEzek-b (4Q74), Qumran Cave 4
readings.en: and their likeness over the heads of the living creature, a dome
readings.plain: was their likeness, a dome

why: The Masoretic Text gives a clear sense and the Greek agrees with it. The scroll's 'their likeness' differs by one letter (a final mem) and may be a slip or a different tradition.
b: Only 4QEzek-b has this part of the verse among the scrolls read for this part. The reading changes the grammar little: in both, a dome-like surface is above the living creatures.

a: the Israelites, to nations of rebels who have rebelled against me
t: 'Rebellious nations' or the house of Israel
p: The Greek has no 'nations': it says 'the house of Israel, who embitter me'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: to the sons of Israel, to nations of rebels
readings.plain: the Israelites, to nations of rebels who have rebelled against me

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete)
readings.orig: πρὸς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ Ἰσραήλ, τοὺς παραπικραίνοντάς με
readings.en: to the house of Israel, those who embitter me
readings.plain: the house of Israel, who have turned bitter against me

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading: calling Israel 'nations' is odd, and a translator or scribe could easily have smoothed it. The Greek's shorter text may be a simplification, so the Plain follows the Hebrew, as in the note.
b: No scroll preserves this verse among those read for this part. The Greek verb translates the Hebrew root of 'rebel' (marah) elsewhere in the book, so the translator may have read the same word and left out 'nations' to avoid the oddity.

a: and I sat where they were living. I sat there
p: The written text and the marginal reading differ; the Greek has no Tel-abib.

readings.w: Qere (the reading marked in the margin of the Leningrad Codex; the Leningrad text is pointed to match it)
readings.en: and I sat; they were sitting there
readings.plain: and I sat where they were living. I sat there

readings.w: Ketiv (the consonants written in the text of the Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and where they were sitting there
readings.plain: and where they were living, I sat there

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete)
readings.orig: καὶ εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὴν αἰχμαλωσίαν μετέωρος, καὶ περιῆλθον τοὺς κατοικοῦντας ἐπὶ τοῦ ποταμοῦ τοῦ Χοβάρ
readings.en: and I went into the captivity, lifted up, and went around those living by the river Chobar
readings.plain: I went among the exiles, shaken, and went around those living by the Kebar canal

why: The marginal reading gives a smooth sentence with a verb, and the written text, 'and where they were sitting there', seems to lack one. Either way Ezekiel sits where the exiles live for seven days. The Greek reads the verse differently throughout and does not name Tel-abib, so it gives no help with the Ketiv or the Qere; the Plain follows the Hebrew.
b: The two Hebrew readings differ by one word: the Ketiv has 'asher ('where') and the Qere has 'esheb ('I sat'). The meaning is the same: he took his place among them. The Greek has a different construction and no place name, and no scroll preserves the verse.

p: The Greek has 190 days here and in 4:9; the Hebrew has 390 in both. The two verses go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 11QEzek (11Q4) preserves the plural 'hundreds' with 'ninety' in 4:9, which excludes 190
readings.en: three hundred and ninety days
readings.plain: three hundred and ninety days

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete), in 4:5 and 4:9
readings.en: one hundred and ninety days
readings.plain: one hundred and ninety days

why: The Hebrew has the same number twice, and a Qumran scroll shows the plural 'hundreds' in 4:9. The Greek's 190 may come from an earlier Hebrew text or from a translator who wanted the numbers to match years: 190 + 40 = 230. The Plain follows the Hebrew with the Qumran witness.
b: In Swete's Greek, 4:4 also has a number, 'a hundred and fifty days', which the Hebrew lacks, so the Greek numbers are not consistent with each other. The Hebrew 390 + 40 = 430 matches the years in Egypt (Exodus 12:40), which some commentators think is intended; the Hebrew 390 also does not fit the dated space between 1:2 and 8:1 (see the note at 4:5). Qumran: 11QEzek (4:3-6, 9-10) and 1QEzek (4:16-5:1) are the scrolls that preserve this part; the number in 4:5 itself is partly restored, so it should not be cited as the scroll's reading.

p: Goes together with the variant at 4:5.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 11QEzek (11Q4) has 'hundreds and ninety' here
readings.en: three hundred and ninety days
readings.plain: three hundred and ninety days

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete)
readings.en: one hundred and ninety days
readings.plain: one hundred and ninety days

b: The scroll's 'hundreds and ninety' is visible here (only the 'three' is restored).

a: you have not even done as the rulings of the nations
p: Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac are reported to lack the last 'not'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete), which has the same negative
readings.orig: וּכְמִשְׁפְּטֵי הַגּוֹיִם אֲשֶׁר סְבִיבוֹתֵיכֶם לֹא עֲשִׂיתֶם
readings.en: and according to the rulings of the nations around you you have not done
readings.plain: you have not even done as the rulings of the nations

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac, as reported in the apparatus of the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia
readings.en: and according to the rulings of the nations around you you have done
readings.plain: you have done as the rulings of the nations around you require

why: The Hebrew and the Greek agree on the 'not', and the reading without it is the one that matches 11:12, so it may be an effort to make the two verses agree. The Plain follows the Hebrew; the note at 5:7 sets out the other ways of resolving the clash.
b: Only the apparatus as quoted by the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia was used for the second reading; the manuscripts themselves were not seen.

p: The Hebrew passive 'I was broken' is odd; the Vulgate has the active 'I broke', the Greek 'I swore'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); the KJV and WEB follow it
readings.en: how I was broken with their heart
readings.plain: I was broken by

readings.w: Vulgate (Jerome)
readings.en: I crushed their heart
readings.plain: I broke their heart

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete)
readings.en: I have sworn to their heart
readings.plain: I swore against their heart

why: The Hebrew passive is unusual but makes sense: the LORD is hurt by his people's unfaithfulness, as a husband would be. The Vulgate reads the active, which needs the nun dropped from the verb (shavarti for nishbarti). The Greek's 'I swore' comes from a Hebrew text that differed by a letter or two (compare nishba'ti, 'I swore'); it may also have been chosen because the passive is hard. The Plain follows the Hebrew.
b: The sense of the Hebrew is that the LORD himself is injured, which fits the marriage language of Hosea and Ezekiel 16.
